articles.title: Elon Musk's Cybercab has no steering wheel, pedals or mirrors; US safety regulators open audit of about 1,000 cars over Tesla's self-certification
articles.summary: Tech News News: ​Tesla's race to deploy its Cybercab robotaxis is testing US vehicle-safety rules. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, this comes as the.
articles.body: ​Tesla's race to deploy its Cybercab robotaxis is testing US vehicle-safety rules. According to a report by the news agency Reuters, this comes as the Elon Musk-led electric-car maker begins offering paid rides in two-seat vehicles that operate without a steering wheel, pedals or conventional mirrors.​Just hours after an event in downtown Austin, Texas, marking the rollout, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said it had opened an audit of about 1,000 Cybercab vehicles, the Reuters report noted. The review will examine how Tesla determined that the cars comply with federal vehicle-safety regulations.​US regulations on the commercialisation of vehicles that fail to meet federal safety standards were mostly created with human-driven cars in mind and require manual operation. However, these regulations have loopholes, and Tesla CEO Elon Musk is well aware of them.​Amid a crowd of Tesla fans and social media influencers in downtown Austin, Tesla added Cybercabs to its robotaxi fleet, which already operates the company's best-selling Model Y SUVs. Tesla said Cybercab rides would be open to everyone, and executives discussed pricing plans.​The golden-coloured Cybercab, fitted with butterfly doors, is central to Musk's strategy of relying on self-driving software and robotics. That strategy has helped push Tesla's stock valuation to about $1.4 trillion, exceeding the combined value of several of the world's largest automakers.​Unlike many other countries, the US does not generally require automakers to obtain regulatory clearance for a new vehicle model and its technology before putting it on public roads. Instead, manufacturers can deploy vehicles by self-certifying that they meet federal safety standards.​"I don't think there is a reasonable interpretation that can be made to suggest that the Cybercab can comply with the Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards," Michael Brooks, executive director of the Center for Auto Safety, a consumer advocacy group told Reuters.​At the same time, NHTSA is moving to change vehicle-safety standards and is separately drafting rules intended to accommodate driverless vehicles. Industry experts have said those changes are likely to take longer to take effect than the timeline Musk has promised for the Cybercab.​Musk has previously shown a willingness to challenge regulations. "Tesla historically has tested limits and pushed boundaries on regulations," said Philip Koopman, a Carnegie Mellon University engineering professor and autonomous-vehicle safety expert. "I fully expect Tesla to test the limits."​Koopman said Musk could come up with a "creative interpretation" of vehicle regulation, say that Cybercabs comply with federal standards and "flood the market" with them. "That could take NHTSA or state regulators years to resolve. Meanwhile, Tesla could be operating on public roads."​A vehicle without conventional controls​The Cybercab manufacturing process began in April, and Musk has promised that the production rate will increase exponentially either late this year or early next year. In addition, Musk said the Cybercab would cost less than $30,000 when it was introduced in 2024.​Furthermore, Tesla has started providing its customers with a robotaxi service in Texas and Florida; however, this service is only available with the Model Y SUV. The vehicles are autonomous; however, they still have manual controls, which certain regulations and manufacturers mandate.​The Cybercab's uniqueness lies in its lack of controls found in conventional vehicles. Specialists have raised concerns about the autonomous driving capabilities of vehicles manufactured by Tesla.Tesla has said its Full Self-Driving software, which powers the Cybercab, is up to 10 times safer than human drivers. The company's Austin robotaxi service has also operated without a fatal accident. However, Reuters interviews with several former Tesla employees who trained the company's self-driving software found that it continued to struggle with basic driving manoeuvres.​"No public information about Tesla's capabilities suggests that Tesla is anywhere close to being able to safely and reliably deploy an automated driving system over the wide range of conditions that would be required for a vehicle without conventional controls," said Bryant Walker Smith, a University of South Carolina law professor focused on autonomous-driving regulation.​The issue concerns federal safety standards for automobiles drafted for manually operated cars. The issue arises because cars with automated driving systems lack some controls needed to comply with the standards.​A path to public roads​For vehicles that do not comply with federal safety standards, NHTSA has an exemption process that allows automakers to seek permission for limited deployment. That route, however, currently caps deployment at 2,500 vehicles a year.​Tesla's engineering chief Lars Moravy said on social media platform X earlier this year that the Cybercab would not be subject to that cap, although he did not explain why. NHTSA has previously said Tesla had not applied for an exemption.​That has led to speculation that Tesla may have instead chosen to self-certify the Cybercab, as Koopman suggested.​A precedent already exists involving another autonomous vehicle without conventional driving controls. Amazon's Zoox, which is developing a vehicle with two bench seats facing each other and no driving controls, also attempted to use the self-certification route.​Zoox declared its car safe to operate, but it retracted that statement when NHTSA decided to investigate. About a year later, in July, Zoox received a government exemption.​Any dispute between NHTSA and Tesla over the Cybercab's self-certification could eventually end up in court, according to three former senior NHTSA officials who spoke to Reuters before Thursday's event. "It does happen from time to time and NHTSA, importantly, has not always won these cases," one of the former officials said.​Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Putin, Xi and Iran's Pezeshkian descend on India for high-stakes BRICS summit amid escalating global tensions
articles.summary: Presidents of Iran, Russia and China converge on New Delhi for the BRICS summit as India navigates competing interests amid Middle East and Ukraine wars.
articles.body: All eyes will be on New Delhi this weekend, as the presidents of Iran, Russia and China gather in India for the 18th BRICS summit. The meeting comes at a critical time as conflicts roil the Middle East and Europe, putting the bloc to one of its biggest tests since its founding 20 years ago. The Sept. 12-13 summit comes more than six months after the Middle East war broke out between the U.S. and Iran, and at a time when regional tensions are again spiking. It follows the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit earlier this month, where several of the same leaders met. The BRICS alliance was established in 2006 by founding members Brazil, Russia, India and China, and has since expanded to include nations such as Iran, Egypt, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. INDIA'S MODI-IRAN MEETING COMES AMID US WARNINGS OF SANCTIONS ON TEHRAN'S TRADING PARTNERS At the forefront are Iran-India relations, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Prime Minister Narendra Modi likely to highlight trade, connectivity, energy cooperation and regional developments. The two leaders are meeting less than two weeks after reaffirming their "longstanding" strategic partnership. In the face of an economic onslaught from Washington, Tehran has been working to deepen ties with Moscow and Beijing. In its latest attempt at securing a critical economic lifeline, Iran is seeking membership in the BRICS New Development Bank. The effort comes as many of Iran's largest remaining economic partners, including China, India, Russia and the UAE, will all be represented in New Delhi, giving Tehran a rare opportunity to engage several key trading partners collectively, just as the U.S. ramps up sanctions pressure. CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS Also in focus is China. President Xi Jinping will be visiting India for the first time in seven years. The high-stakes trip marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between India and China after a deadly military clash in 2020 along their disputed Himalayan border. A bilateral meeting between Modi and Xi is expected to focus on maintaining that normalization while expanding economic engagement, making it one of the summit's most closely watched sidelines meetings. Then there is Russia. President Vladimir Putin met Modi on Friday in a pre-summit bilateral meeting. It marks Putin's first trip to India since the Ukraine war began four years ago. Energy and defense are expected to dominate the agenda after the Russian president criticized American tariffs as "illegal" and "unacceptable." Just earlier this week, the Kremlin touted expanding energy ties, saying India's imports of Russian energy have reached a "new record" every month. Moscow has also said Russia understands India's position on the war in Ukraine and that it "to a great extent corresponds" with Russia's own position, while calling on India to facilitate a peaceful resolution. IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS The meeting also comes days after Putin publicly welcomed the UAE’s role in facilitating discussions over the Ukraine war, highlighting Abu Dhabi's increasingly influential diplomatic role as another major BRICS participant. Saudi Arabia will also be watched after Iran-backed Houthi militia renewed attacks on its cities earlier this week. Both the UAE and Saudi Arabia have become increasingly central to India's Gulf strategy. The summit also comes as New Delhi attempts to navigate widening divisions between Tehran and Abu Dhabi after the UAE cut off commercial and financial dealings with Iran. The suspension has already squeezed Indian exporters, as Dubai has long served as a key commercial hub for India's trade with Iran, giving India a direct economic incentive. The BRICS summit will be a major test of India's diplomatic mettle in more ways than one, as the nation finds itself balancing competing interests from Washington, Tehran, Moscow, Beijing and the Gulf while trying to forge unity among BRICS members. "New Delhi’s leadership of BRICS is ultimately an exercise in managing contradiction. The biggest challenge is to ensure BRICS remains a platform for advancing Global South priorities rather than becoming an arena for great-power rivalry, Harsh V. Pant, vice president at Observer Research Foundation, told Fox News Digital. "New Delhi is trying to keep the focus on practical cooperation — from energy security to connectivity and development — rather than ideological confrontation." FROM BEAR HUGS TO HANDSHAKES: HOW INDIA LOST ITS EDGE WITH TRUMP WHILE PAKISTAN QUIETLY GAINED GROUND Building a unified position among BRICS members will be a complex task for India, especially given the sharp geopolitical divergences among member states, such as the U.S-China rivalry, the Russia-Ukraine war and tensions involving Iran, Israel and the UAE. Modi will have to balance championing his own priorities with the summit's, as well as toeing the line to avoid an anti-U.S. tilt. "The balancing act reflects India's broader foreign policy, which seeks to maintain strong ties with Washington while continuing to engage Moscow, Beijing and Tehran," Pant said. Throughout the conflict, India has sought to position itself as a voice for dialogue while avoiding taking sides, emphasizing themes of resilience, sustainability, cooperation and innovation. But experts warn that failure to reach consensus would expose the limits of the expanded BRICS grouping, whose broader membership has also imported longstanding regional rivalries. Though major Western powers are absent, analysts say the alliance is not to be dismissed. Every ceasefire in this conflict has involved mediation by BRICS members or partners, and leaders gathering in New Delhi are expected to explore whether the forum can once again provide diplomatic momentum after recent attempts to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran stalled. "Hosting the BRICS summit in New Delhi offers India an important opportunity to demonstrate the logic of its multi-alignment at a time when global politics is becoming increasingly polarized, "Pant said. "By bringing together countries such as China, Russia, Iran and the Gulf states while simultaneously deepening its partnerships with the United States and the Quad, India is signaling that it does not accept the binary choices imposed by great-power rivalry." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The stakes extend beyond diplomacy as disruptions from the war have disproportionately affected developing nations. India, the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer, has already suffered energy and inflation hits. "The real measure of India’s success will therefore be its ability to keep BRICS sufficiently inclusive and functional to address Global South priorities while preventing geopolitical divisions from paralyzing the grouping," Pant said.

articles.title: US prices remain high as fuel costs squeeze household budgets
articles.summary: Prices in the US rose 3.4% in the 12 months to August,  according to the latest official report on inflation.
articles.body:
Prices in the US rose by 3.4% in the year to August, with the cost of living pushed up by higher gasoline prices, official figures show.

The overall inflation rate was unchanged from July, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

It comes ahead of the Federal Reserve making its latest interest rate decision next week, with growing expectations they will be increased in a bid to slow the rate at which prices are rising.

US household budgets have come under mounting pressure, especially at the fuel pumps, with a gallon of diesel hitting a new all-time high of more than $6 on average on Friday.

The spike in fuel prices has been driven by higher global oil prices , caused by supply disruptions as a result of the US-Iran war. The price of benchmark Brent crude oil is hovering above $100 a barrel following recent escalations in the conflict.

As well as directly driving up costs at the pumps, higher oil prices can also make transporting goods more expensive. Such costs can be passed down to consumers through steeper prices for food and other staples, pushing up the overall cost of living.

The BLS said gasoline prices rose 3.9% last month alone, accounting for more than a third of inflation overall. Wages are also failing to keep up with the rising cost of living, with separate figures showing real average hourly earnings fell by 0.3% over the past year.

There are increasing expectations that interest rates will be hiked given the current inflation picture, strong jobs market and President Donald Trump saying he does not think oil prices will come down until the war with Iran ends, which he expects to happen after November's elections.

Fed chair Kevin Warsh has been tight-lipped on any future decisions, but his comments that the central bank's focus should be on slowing price rises has further fuelled expectations of a rise.

According to data from CME Group, 85% of traders are now betting on rates being raised by a quarter percentage point next week.

Interest rates could rise again across the world – here's why

Skyler Weinand, chief investment officer at Regan Capital based in Dallas, said while inflation was in line with expectations, it was "still too hot and the Federal Reserve's hands are tied".

"A rate hike next week is all but assured. Consumer prices are going in the wrong direction and remain significantly higher than the Fed's 2% target."

Interest rates have been left on hold for five meetings in a row, at between 3.5% and 3.75%. Higher rates are a tool used by central banks aiming to slow the pace of price rises.

By pushing up the cost of borrowing for things such as mortgages, loans and credit cards, it is hoped consumers will spend less and the rate of price increases will slow. Increased rates can encourage people to save money by increasing their potential returns.

Jamie Hagen, president of Hell Bent Xpress, a family-owned trucking company in South Dakota, told the BBC's World Business Report podcast that higher oil prices were hurting his business

"I've already invested in new equipment. We thought the economy was gonna start humming and now everybody's paused. Like someone turned the faucet off," he said.

"The calls aren't coming in, the freight is slowing down drastically because there's just no money left for it. People aren't buying things and shippers aren't making things."

articles.title: US federal court rules residents of a Mississippi town with a population of 150,000, don't have a constitutional right to lead-free water
articles.summary: US News: For residents of Jackson, Mississippi, the question is simple yet difficult to answer: can people expect the water flowing from their taps to be safe .
articles.body: For residents of Jackson, Mississippi, the question is simple yet difficult to answer: can people expect the water flowing from their taps to be safe to drink? A federal appeals court has now delivered a striking legal answer: not as a constitutional right. The Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the US Constitution does not guarantee Americans a right to clean drinking water, rejecting a lawsuit brought by residents of Jackson over years of problems with the city's water system. The decision upheld a lower court's dismissal of the case.What did Jackson citizens allege?The case was brought by a group of Jackson residents in 2022, who alleged that the city allowed lead to enter the municipal water system and then lied to residents saying the water was safe, though they knew it was not. “Knowing what is in our water is fundamental to protecting public health,” Caroline Leary, general counsel at the U.S.-based nonprofit Environmental Working Group, told Mongabay by email.Jackson is home to roughly 150,000 people. Nearly a quarter of them are children under 18 who are particularly vulnerable to the potentially lifelong toxic impacts of lead exposure including seizures, lowered IQ, impaired brain development and even death.The plaintiffs alleged that several of their children have been diagnosed with lead poisoning and now require special educational, medical, sociological, occupational and disability services. The plaintiffs also argued that exposure to contaminated water and the failure to be informed about the risks violated their 14th Amendment due process right to bodily integrity.Jackson's water system has faced serious problems for years. Residents have dealt with boil-water advisories, low water pressure and periods when water was unavailable altogether. The city's major water crisis in 2022 followed years of infrastructure and treatment problems.The residents' legal argument went beyond saying that officials had failed in their duties. They sought recognition of a constitutional right to be protected from contaminated water and a constitutional right to receive accurate information from public officials about the condition of their water.The appeals court rejected both arguments.What did the court say?A November 2025 ruling by a three-judge panel of the Fifth U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals allowed these claims against the city to proceed. However, on September 4, 2026, the full court ruled against the plaintiffs, stating that the court could not recognise two new constitutional rights, “the right to be free from exposure to contaminated water and the right to accurate information from public officials.”The Fifth Circuit's majority said the plaintiffs were effectively asking the judiciary to establish new constitutional rights that do not have a foundation in the nation's legal history and tradition. The court stated that the Constitution does not guarantee clean water and said municipalities are not constitutionally required to provide water treatment, sewerage or waste-management services in a reasonably competent manner.That does not mean the court declared contaminated water acceptable or ruled that governments have no obligations concerning drinking water. Rather, it found that the Constitution itself does not provide the particular right the residents were asking the court to recognise.The court acknowledged the seriousness of the residents' allegations and said it was sympathetic to the injuries they could suffer. But it concluded that sympathy could not transform the residents' claims into constitutional violations.Instead, the judges pointed toward other avenues, including tort claims, political action and efforts to hold public officials accountable through elections.Why Jackson's water crisis mattersJackson's case is rooted in a much larger infrastructure problem. The city's water system has struggled with ageing pipes, treatment facilities, staffing and financial pressures. Federal authorities have previously identified significant deficiencies in the system, while residents have repeatedly faced warnings about the safety and reliability of their water.In 2022, Jackson was thrust into another major water crisis after problems at its main treatment facility contributed to a widespread loss of water pressure. The crisis left residents struggling to obtain safe and reliable running water. The city's predominantly Black population has also made the water crisis part of a broader debate about environmental justice and the distribution of public infrastructure funding.The NAACP has separately accused Mississippi state authorities of diverting federal money intended for Jackson's water infrastructure to predominantly white communities. A civil rights complaint filed in 2022 alleged that this contributed to persistent gaps in access to safe drinking water. The organisation later filed a lawsuit against state officials in 2025.Americans still have protections under federal and state laws governing drinking water quality. The federal government regulates public drinking water through laws including the Safe Drinking Water Act, while states and local authorities have their own responsibilities and regulations. The court itself noted that state and federal authorities have been working to improve Jackson's water quality through regulations, investigations and compliance plans. “Plaintiffs have not been left to go at it alone,” the court said. “The State of Mississippi and federal government have worked for years, and continue today, to improve the city of Jackson’s drinking water quality through regulations, investigations, and compliance plans.”Water is one of the most basic requirements of daily life. People generally do not think about constitutional law when they turn on a kitchen tap. They expect water to be available and safe.But Jackson's residents took their fight into federal court because, for many of them, reliable drinking water had become anything but routine.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1986, Warren Buffett bought a 400-acre Nebraska farm for $280,000; nearly 40 years later, his son is farming there and championing soil conservation instead of managing billions
articles.summary: US News: Warren Buffett spent decades building one of the world's biggest business empires. His middle son, Howard Graham Buffett, chose a very different path..
articles.body: Warren Buffett spent decades building one of the world's biggest business empires. His middle son, Howard Graham Buffett, chose a very different path. Rather than following his father into investment and finance, Howard became a farmer and conservationist. For much of his adult life, he has worked with corn and soybeans, farmed in Nebraska and Illinois, and focused on conservation practices designed to protect soil. He has also been involved with research farms studying methods including no-till agriculture and soil health.Warren Buffett bought a 400-acre farm and rented it to his sonIn 1986, Warren Buffett bought a 400-acre farm in Nebraska, about 50 miles north of Omaha, for $280,000. He bought it from the FDIC after the collapse in Midwestern farmland prices and later rented it to Howard. In his own account of the investment, Warren Buffett said his son loved farming and helped him estimate the farm's expected production and operating costs. Howard's arrangement with his father was anything but a conventional family deal. According to the Howard G. Buffett Foundation, the rental arrangement included 5% a year plus either 22% or 26% of the farm's gross receipts, depending on Howard's weight. The threshold was 182.5 pounds.If Howard was at or below that weight, the percentage was lower. If he went above it, the percentage increased. Howard spoke about the unusual arrangement in a Fortune interview, explaining that his father owned the land and that he paid him a percentage of the farm's gross income as rent. He also joked about the weight clause, describing it as the “Buffett family version of going to Weight Watchers.” The arrangement reflected Warren Buffett's approach to business.He chose fields over financeHoward did have experience in the corporate world. He has served on Berkshire Hathaway's board since 1993 and has also held senior corporate positions. But farming remained a major part of his professional life. His work has largely centred on corn and soybeans, while his interests have expanded into conservation agriculture, food security and sustainable farming practices. He has farmed in Nebraska and Illinois, including the Nebraska property bought by his father and a 1,500-acre farm in Pana, Illinois.Why no-till farming matters to Howard BuffettOne of the practices closely associated with Howard's agricultural work is no-till farming. The method reduces mechanical disturbance of the soil rather than repeatedly turning it over with conventional tillage. Howard has used no-till methods for decades and has spoken publicly about their potential benefits. In an interview with Mid-America Farmer Grower, he said, “I'm a real believer in no-till because I've seen it work.” He also discussed lower fuel use and fewer tractor hours as practical benefits of the method.His foundation has supported research into conservation agriculture, including large-scale trials examining no-till and conventional tillage and their effects on agricultural production and soil.His Illinois farm became part of that experimentHoward's agricultural work eventually extended well beyond the Nebraska property. He works a 1,500-acre farm in Pana, Illinois, where his interest in conservation agriculture has played an important role. His foundation has also supported and operated research farms in the United States, including work in Illinois, Nebraska and Arizona. The work reflects Howard's broader interest in food security and agricultural research.The billionaire's son who still wanted to be a farmerHoward's decision is particularly striking because of the family he was born into. His father is Warren Buffett, one of the world's best-known investors and the longtime leader of Berkshire Hathaway. Howard, however, built much of his professional life around farming rather than investment management. That choice also shaped the role his father envisioned for him at Berkshire. Warren Buffett did not plan for Howard to become the conglomerate's chief executive. Instead, he has long associated his son with a possible future role as non-executive chairman, helping protect Berkshire's culture without running its day-to-day operations.Howard has previously made clear that he did not want that responsibility to mean abandoning farming. “As long as I can keep farming,” he said when discussing the proposed role in an earlier 60 Minutes interview.Berkshire Hathaway's succession planBerkshire Hathaway's succession plan has now moved into a new phase. Greg Abel became Berkshire Hathaway's CEO on January 1, 2026, succeeding Warren Buffett. Warren Buffett remains chairman. Howard's potential future role is different. Berkshire's 2026 proxy statement says Warren Buffett believes that, after his death, it would be prudent for a member of the Buffett family to serve as non-executive chairman. Howard Buffett has long been associated with that succession plan, but the final decision will belong to Berkshire's board.Howard would not be expected to run Berkshire's businesses or direct its investments as non-executive chairman. Instead, the role would be focused on helping protect the culture his father spent decades building. The person who may eventually help safeguard Warren Buffett's Berkshire legacy, therefore, is not a career financier. He is a farmer.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: France sends Rafales on 40,000-km global mission to project power from Arctic to Indo-Pacific
articles.summary: International News: France has launched a 40-day global air-power mission, sending Rafale fighter jets on a 40,000-kilometre journey across the Arctic, Indo-Pacific and M.
articles.body: France has launched a 40-day global air-power mission, sending Rafale fighter jets on a 40,000-kilometre journey across the Arctic, Indo-Pacific and Middle East in a major demonstration of its long-range military reach and strategic partnerships.According to the Associated Press, the Pegase 26 mission will involve four Rafales supported by three A330 MRTT tanker aircraft, two A400M transport aircraft and around 300 personnel. The deployment will cross three continents and include nine stopovers as French forces train and operate alongside strategic partners.The mission, which began from Istres air base in southern France on September 8, is designed to demonstrate France's ability to rapidly deploy combat aircraft far from its territory while maintaining operations through aerial refuelling and logistical support.French deputy defence minister Alice Rufo said the deployment is also intended to strengthen interoperability with partner countries.“In practical terms, we fly together, we land together, we work together,” Rufo said, adding that forces must be “immediately interoperable” if they are required to respond jointly to a threat.The route of the flightThe French aircrafts will take new northern route toward the Indo-Pacific. The aircraft first flew over the Arctic, passing through Greenland and Canada before reaching Alaska, in what the French military says is the first time the Pegase deployment has used this route.From Alaska, the French aircraft will continue across the Indo-Pacific, with planned stopovers in Japan, South Korea, Indonesia and India. The deployment will then move westward toward the Middle East, with stops in Qatar and Réunion, before concluding in Egypt.Significance of the exerciseThe Arctic leg is a key feature of this year's mission. Pegase 26 commander Gen Julien Sabéné told the Associated Press that it is “the first time we are heading up north, over Greenland, toward Alaska.”He said France needs to explore alternative routes to the Indo-Pacific because “we never know in case we need to go in the Indo-Pacific region,” adding that the northern corridor provides “another option, going up north.”The exercise comes six months after President Emmanuel Macron offered to discuss extending France's nuclear deterrence umbrella to European partners amid concerns over US security commitments.According to he Associated Press, Pegase 26 is not a nuclear exercise, but some Rafale variants can carry nuclear-armed missiles, while pilots from France's strategic air force are participating. The fighters are carrying only mock conventional weapons during the mission.

articles.title: I witnessed the horror of 9/11 firsthand. Here's what I learned about God, courage and life
articles.summary: A 9/11 survivor who witnessed the World Trade Center attack from an adjacent building shares how that day led her to become an FBI special agent.
articles.body: Tuesday, 8:46 a.m., September 11, 2001, changed my life — and the lives of millions of others — forever. Nineteen hijackers from the terrorist organization al Qaeda carried out the devil’s work, resulting in the murder of 2,977 innocent souls who were never able to fulfill the measure of their creation. I witnessed the horror unfold up close while working at Merrill Lynch on the top floor of the World Financial Center, adjacent to the World Trade Center (WTC) in New York City. When I heard the loudest explosion, I rushed to the window and saw a gaping hole, chunks of the silver metallic building falling like confetti, massive flames and black smoke billowing from the North Tower (1 WTC). I could not process what I was seeing. I had walked through 1 WTC only an hour earlier. My first thought was: "People are dying up there." My heart was crushed as the terror continued. After I watched the second plane slam into the South Tower (2 WTC), I knew we were under attack. I frantically escaped my building. Amid the pandemonium, a sobering question came to mind. For a moment, time stood still, and I asked myself: If I were to die today, am I prepared to meet my Maker? Am I ready to die? FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE Through the fear and terror, I experienced a glimmer of peace as I dug deep to make sense of the mayhem. One thing I knew for certain: I was a child of God, and He loved me. I felt that calm reassurance even in the darkness. There was hope. I instantly knew I was at the WTC for a reason. Right then, I vowed that I would stand as a witness for God, serve others and serve our great nation. I stayed true to that vow and left the lucrative financial industry in 2009 to serve as an FBI special agent. 9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD' I witnessed the best and worst of humanity on 9/11. articles.title: Former Mets pitcher Al Leiter tells his harrowing 9/11 story of a quiet trip turned tragedy
articles.summary: Al Leiter recalls his harrowing 9/11 morning, from sneaking home to walk his daughter to school to watching the twin towers burn from a cab.
articles.body: On September 11, 2001, former New York Mets pitcher Al Leiter was trying to pull off a quiet personal mission before pitching in Pittsburgh that night. Decades later, appearing on OutKick's "The Craig Carton Show," Leiter recalled the events of that fateful morning. His story began with a father wanting to be present for a family milestone. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Despite a scheduled game in Pittsburgh, Leiter quietly flew home to New York without informing team management. "I wanted to be there for my daughter's first grade," Leiter said. "She was scared. You know, 'We'll be there, honey.' And I'm like playing a long time, I'm probably 15, 16 years in the big leagues, whatever. And I knew if it wasn't Pittsburgh, US Air had like a flight like every hour, was like a shuttle. Drop her off, get on the plane." He acknowledged breaking routine without his bosses knowing: "I never had done this, Craig. I can't believe I actually did it. I don't know if I did it like Bobby Valentine and Steve Phillips didn't know about it." GEORGE W BUSH RECALLS MOMENT WITH DEREK JETER BEFORE NERVE-WRACKING PITCH AT YANKEE STADIUM AFTER 9/11 After walking his daughter to school, Leiter sat on the tarmac at LaGuardia Airport as initial reports trickled in. "The pilot says, 'Oh, it looks like a news helicopter by the [World] Trade Center. We're about ready to take off,'" Leiter recalled. "And then not five minutes later, we're going back to the airport. Get your stuff. New York airspace is closed, LaGuardia is closed, evacuate." Even after evacuating, the true scale of the crisis hadn't set in. "I still think we're gonna play. At that time, you know, we don't know what they're like." Determined to reach his team, Leiter hailed a cab to head toward Philadelphia for an alternate flight. "I called Jay Harts. I'm, 'Jay, you got to get me a flight. I'm going to Philly,'" Leiter recalled. "I have a female Pakistani cab driver. When do you ever get a female, like, and she's crying. I'm like, 'Can you take me to Philadelphia? I'll pay you.' And I'm pissed off. I'm mad. I'm sad. So going over to Triborough Bridge, the towers are burning." As New York City shut down, Leiter rerouted north up the Major Deegan Expressway. "They closed off New York City. I was going to go up to Tappan Zee over to go down through New Jersey to get to Philly to get on a plane to pitch that night," Leiter said. "By the time I'm on the D again, going north of Yankee Stadium, heading up to Tappan Zee, radio's on and the Pentagon just got hit." 9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD' Leiter immediately called then-general manager Steve Phillips. "I called Steve Phillips. I said, 'Steve, I'm sorry, but like, I'm pretty sure we're not playing baseball, right?'" Leiter added. "It's like, 'Don't worry about it.'" Reflecting on the contrast of that morning, Leiter described the weight of the day. "I tell you that story because you know it was so bizarrely unique for like the balls that I had actually to do that, and then that was the day of the most heinous terrorist act in the history of our country," he said. Looking back decades later, Leiter emphasized that while public discussion surrounding the tragedy shifts, historical reality does not. "Every year it's like my story doesn't change, right? Like history doesn't change. Although now what we're seeing, like you know I read the paper about like there were 19 Al-Qaeda guys that took down four planes. Like I'm reading stuff, there's like the story is changing. What are we doing here, right? My story's not changed." Leiter cautioned against efforts to reshape the narrative around the tragedy. "I think a narrative that is out there is trying to paint 9/11 in a way that I just disagree with," Leiter said. "That was a heinous terrorist act that killed 3,000 lives, right? Almost 400 firefighters running up there to help people. And so many more." He emphasized that keeping the memory clear remains an essential duty. "It couldn't be a simpler moniker of Never Forget, right?" Leiter stated. "And it's not just a slogan. It's true. Because it's easy, I can see how as time goes on, you start... wait a minute, that happened. Let's not forget that it happened." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. articles.title: Ethiopia planted eucalyptus to fight deforestation; decades later scientists found the trees can threaten springs and water supplies
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Eucalyptus trees were introduced to Ethiopia more than a century ago as the country struggled with shortages of firewood and construction timber. Thei.
articles.body: Eucalyptus trees were introduced to Ethiopia more than a century ago as the country struggled with shortages of firewood and construction timber. Their rapid growth made them an attractive answer to the pressure on natural forests, and later government reforestation programmes encouraged their wider planting. Over time, eucalyptus became one of the most widely planted trees in the country, supplying fuelwood, timber and income while reducing some of the demand that drives deforestation. But decades of expansion have also exposed a difficult trade-off: trees planted to ease pressure on forests can consume substantial amounts of water in areas where supplies are already limited. A 2025 review, ‘Socioeconomic and Environmental Impacts of Eucalyptus Plantations in Ethiopia: An Evaluation of Benefits, Challenges, and Sustainable Practices,’ by Kiros Getachew Belachew and Wondwosson Kibrie Minale, examined these competing effects.How eucalyptus became a solution to Ethiopia’s deforestation problemEucalyptus first arrived in Ethiopia in the late 19th century, when it was planted to address shortages of firewood and construction wood around the capital. Its appeal was straightforward: the trees grow quickly, produce useful timber and can provide a regular source of income for households. As demand for wood increased with population growth, agriculture, construction and energy needs, eucalyptus spread far beyond the areas where it was first planted.The expansion accelerated further during the 1980s, when fast-growing eucalyptus species became part of government re-greening and plantation programmes. According to the review by Belachew and Minale, eucalyptus plantations now cover around 506,000 hectares of Ethiopia. For farmers, the trees can be particularly attractive because they provide marketable wood relatively quickly, while their cultivation can reduce reliance on natural forests for some wood products.That success, however, came with a growing environmental debate. Researchers and communities began reporting concerns about eucalyptus plantations near farmland and water sources, including reduced water availability, declining soil fertility and the displacement of native vegetation.Why the same trees can put pressure on springs and groundwaterThe concern is closely linked to the way eucalyptus grows. Fast-growing trees require substantial amounts of water, and eucalyptus has extensive root systems and high evapotranspiration rates that can draw moisture from the soil and groundwater. The 2025 review found that eucalyptus plantations can alter runoff, reduce soil moisture and decrease groundwater recharge.One finding highlighted in the review is particularly striking. In Ethiopia’s central highlands, converting cultivated land to eucalyptus plantations was associated with a 51.1% decrease in soil moisture and a 48.9% reduction in spring water flow. Research from the Koga watershed in the Amhara Region also found that eucalyptus plantations close to water sources could contribute to springs drying up completely.The effects can become even more pronounced during dry periods. In the Lake Tana Basin, researchers observed substantial groundwater fluctuations associated with eucalyptus plantations. The review reports that evapotranspiration from eucalyptus plantations during dry periods could reach 2,300 millimetres, around 1,400 millimetres more than in areas without eucalyptus.Scientists found that eucalyptus is not simply a “bad” treeThe water concerns do not mean eucalyptus has provided no environmental or economic benefits. In fact, its rapid growth is precisely what made it valuable to Ethiopia in the first place. The trees supply fuelwood and construction material, generate household income and can reduce pressure on native forests by providing an alternative source of wood.Research has also shown that the effects can depend heavily on location and management. A nine-year field study in Ethiopia’s Debre Mawi watershed, for example, found that expanding eucalyptus cover was associated with reductions in runoff and sediment concentrations. The researchers also noted a potential downside: eucalyptus could dry wells during the dry monsoon period, something they said required further investigation.This makes the question less about whether eucalyptus should exist in Ethiopia and more about where and how it should be planted. Planting large stands in water-scarce areas or close to springs can create very different consequences from planting trees in locations where their water demand does not threaten essential supplies.Ethiopia now faces a difficult choice over its fast-growing forestsA newer review published in 2026, ‘Environmental Impacts, Land-Use Trade-Offs, and Sustainable Management Pathways of Eucalyptus Plantation Expansion in Ethiopia,’ by Yohannes Gelaye and Kiros Getachew, reached a similar conclusion. It concluded that eucalyptus plantations generate economic benefits through timber, fuelwood, and household income but can also be a source of water shortage, soil degradation and loss of biodiversity.The authors call for better land use management rather than outright ban of eucalyptus. Some of the proposed methods include agroforestry, mixed planting, especially mixed with indigenous multipurpose trees such as Cordia africana, Faidherbia albida, and Acacia abyssinica. It aims at maximizing the economic benefits from the fast-growing tree without having adverse effects on the environment.This is a very surprising lesson from the Ethiopian experience on reforestation. The planting of trees may help deal with the shortage of timber and minimize deforestation of natural forests, but having more trees does not always mean having more water or healthy ecosystem. In landscapes where springs, groundwater and farmland depend on limited moisture, the species chosen, and where it is planted, can matter just as much as the number of trees put into the ground.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: The vanishing pharmacy of the Sundarbans
articles.summary: As rising seas push salt into the world’s largest mangrove, traditional medicinal plants are being lost.
articles.body:
Koyra Upazila, Bangladesh – The Shakbaria river’s low tide has pulled the water back, exposing a wide, slippery mudbank between Suranjan Raptan and the edge of the Sundarbans, the world’s largest tidal mangrove forest.

For most of his life, Suranjan has relied on this forest as his pharmacy. He rises before the sun, crosses into the mangroves in a small boat and walks barefoot through the clay-mud jungle for hours, carrying a knife to cut the leaves, roots and bark he uses to make medicines.

Today, the 40-year-old traditional healer, or kabiraj, has come to borrow his uncle’s boat.

“Uncle, are you home?” he calls from outside the house.

Chapal Raptan, Suranjan’s uncle and a honey collector, is a medium-built man with sharp features.

“Suranjan? Come in and sit,” Chapal Raptan answers, his voice hoarse. “I worked in the rain yesterday; now I have a cold, so I’m resting.”

“Sad news,” Suranjan replies. “Drink hot tea with tulsi leaves and honey. It will help. I won’t sit now; I’m heading to the forest to bring back some plants. I want to take your boat.”

“Okay, uncle. Rest well. If you feel worse, I’ll send medicine,” Suranjan says as he sets off.

Beyond the courtyard lies the road, then the Shakbaria river, and across it, the Sundarbans.

Suranjan finds the overturned boat and lowers it into the water. Leaves and fruits from the forest have gathered on the muddy bank. His feet sink deep into the sticky mud. He climbs into the boat, dangling his legs over the side to wash them, and the wind pushes him across small waves towards the forest.

Stepping into the Sundarbans, the smell of wet mud and salt fills the air. Mangrove roots twist up from the water like claws. Kingfishers sound sharp notes in the half-light; insects hum and leaves sway in the breeze. Suranjan walks barefoot, saying it allows him to feel the ground and move quietly, and that sandals slip too easily.

“A deer passed here not long ago,” he says, pointing to a small hole in the mud.

“These leaves,” he says at a bush, “boil them when the stomach aches.”

A few steps later, he touches the bark of a tall tree. “Scrape it, mix with water, it helps when the cough won’t go away.”

Then he finds a tall Sundari tree, with dark-green, oval leaves.

“This is the tree that gave the forest its name: Sundarbans. Now it is rare. We are lucky to see it here.”

“Before Cyclone Aila [in 2009], the forest was so dense that sunlight could not enter. Since then, it has thinned. The forest feels empty.”

The change became particularly noticeable around 2015 or 2016, he says, when sunlight began reaching places that had once been heavily shaded and familiar medicinal plants became harder to find.

Today he is looking for a particular tree. He searched for it the last time he came but could not find it. He worries it has disappeared.

Suranjan has been a kabiraj for 21 years. He learned from his father, who learned from his grandfather. Nothing was written down. He was taught how to identify plants, where to find them, which parts to harvest and how to prepare them - knowledge passed through practice and memory.

articles.title: Eight people arrested over Bromley KFC multiple stabbing
articles.summary: A man and seven boys are held on suspicion of attempted murder after four people were stabbed.
articles.body:
Eight people have been questioned on suspicion of attempted murder after a multiple stabbing at a KFC restaurant in south-east London.

The Met Police, ambulance service and air ambulance were called out to reports of an altercation involving several people on Bromley High Street at about 14.15 BST on Thursday.

A 21-year-old man and three boys aged between 14 and 17 were taken to hospital with stab wounds. The man's condition was previously critical but is now not thought to be life-threatening.

The Met said those four, plus four other boys aged between 14 and 17 have since been arrested and remain in custody.

A KFC spokesperson confirmed a "serious incident" had taken place at its Bromley High Street restaurant and that the altercation had begun there.

The firm said it was assisting police and supporting team members and customers.

Following the incident, an eyewitness dining at the branch said a fight broke out and a man wielding a machete ran from the scene.

A local business owner said she had seen a fight spill out onto the street.

The Met Police said officers were working quickly to establish the full circumstances, and there would be an increased police presence in the area.

Detectives are treating the incident as an isolated event.

articles.title: Oxford museum agrees to return remains to Naga ancestral homeland
articles.summary: Oxford's Pitt Rivers Museum will return more than three dozen sets of human remains to the Naga people.
articles.body:
More than three dozen sets of human remains taken during the British colonial rule of India and Myanmar are set to be returned to their ancestral home by a museum.

Skulls and bones belonging to the Naga people of northeastern India and Myanmar - formerly known as Burma - have been displayed at the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford for more than a century.

In 2020, the museum removed all human remains from public display as part of what the it called a "decolonisation process" - including the ancestral Naga remains.

The museum has now announced that a formal decision has been made by the University of Oxford Council to return the 39 ancestral human remains to their homeland.

"They've been here in a foreign land for more than a century," Dr Vihuto Asumi, President of the Sumî Hoho Naga tribe, said of the remains.

"We believe that their spirits are still not at rest - so by doing this, we believe it will bring spiritual healing, not only to the ancestral remains here but to everyone who died during the head-hunting days."

The Pitt Rivers claims to hold the largest collection of Naga artefacts in the world, most of which were acquired during British colonial rule in India and Myanmar.

Many were acquired by John Henry Hutton, a colonial administrator in the Indian Civil Service and an anthropologist, who handed them to the museum more than a century ago.

Among the museum's Naga collection - which contains several thousand items - are 219 items are listed as human remains, 39 ancestral human remains and 178 objects that are thought to contain human hair.

The latest announcement concerns only the ancestral remains, and follows a declaration made by a Naga declaration visiting Oxford in 2025, in which the group requested the objects be returned.

The museum's director, Prof Laura Van Broekhoven, said: "It has been a long journey to get to this moment."

"We know that this week will be one where we will feel both grief and sadness when looking back on that past, and also where hope is possible as we work towards reconciliation and healing."

Following the decision, the Pitt Rivers is now organising an official handover ceremony involving a Naga delegation.

The Naga will then accompany the remains of their ancestors home, with some returning for the first time in more than a century.

articles.title: 35 dead, 54 missing after Philippines ferry fire; survivors recount desperate escape
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The death toll from a ferry fire in the Philippines has risen to 35 after more bodies were recovered from the burned wreck on Friday. Another 54 peopl.
articles.body: The death toll from a ferry fire in the Philippines has risen to 35 after more bodies were recovered from the burned wreck on Friday. Another 54 people remain missing, authorities said.The fire broke out on Wednesday night as the passenger ferry was sailing from Manila towards Coron in Palawan province. According to the Philippine coast guard, the vessel was around 7.4 kilometres off the village of Turda, near its destination, when the fire was reported. The cause of the blaze has not yet been determined.There were 43 survivors from the incident, according to AP. Images released by the coast guard showed the gutted interior of the vessel, with what appeared to be charred remains, ashes and burnt metal, including a car.Rescue operations were hampered on Thursday by intense heat and smoke inside the vessel, slowing efforts to reach areas where passengers may have been trapped.Survivor Arnulfo Nokki Villanueva recounted the fire in a video broadcast by News5, saying the blaze spread rapidly.“The fire quickly spread. That's when I dropped to the ground and my back was burned,” he told AP, adding that he escaped by jumping from a window.“I wanted to get a life jacket but failed to get one because people were stepping on me. People were in panic,” Villanueva said.According to the manifest, 134 people were listed as being on board — 117 passengers and 17 crew members. The 53-metre vessel had a capacity for 306 passengers and 27 crew. The coast guard said two passengers listed on the manifest later reported that they had not boarded.Two survivors were tourists from Chile, according to Rachel Conserman, a staffer of the ship's owner, Atienza Interisland Ferries Inc. She said they were recovering from injuries at a hospital in Coron and that no other foreigners were known to have been on board.The shipping company said it was assisting passengers and their families while coordinating with the coast guard and maritime officials to locate those still missing and establish the cause of the fire.Coron, a popular tourist destination known for its clear waters, limestone cliffs and rock formations, relies heavily on ferries for transport across the Philippine archipelago.The country has experienced several major maritime disasters. In 1987, the ferry Dona Paz sank after colliding with a fuel tanker, killing more than 4,300 people in what is regarded as the world's deadliest peacetime maritime disaster.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: First arrest after anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth
articles.summary: A man is arrested on suspicion of violent disorder after the anti-migrant demonstration on Sunday.
articles.body:
A man has been arrested on suspicion of violent disorder and assaulting a police officer following an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth.

Police attended Eastney Marina on Sunday night after hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

A 42-year-old man from Paulsgrove was arrested early Friday morning after officers reviewed video from the protest. He remains in custody.

Assistant Chief Constable Tony Rowlinson called it the "first of several" arrests expected to be made as part of the investigation.

More stories from Hampshire & the Isle of Wight

Listen to the latest news from Hampshire and the Isle of Wight

The police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

Rowlinson said: "We have been consistently clear that violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest and we will investigate incidents like this thoroughly and take robust action against those responsible.

"Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."

He also pointed out the force will not tolerate abuse aimed at police or partner agencies online.

"We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made," Rowlinson said.

"This arrest also sends a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events. If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution."

articles.title: Devastating fire left Birmingham family with only pet gerbils
articles.summary: Paul Stephens was sunbathing in his garden when the devastating fire destroyed his home in Warstock.
articles.body:
When Paul Stephens looks back at the day a fire destroyed his home, he remembers the speed at which everything changed.

He was in his garden sunbathing when flames started spreading towards his house on Gorleston Road in Warstock, Birmingham, on 13 August.

"I was sunbathing in the garden… I could see the smoke… it was about 30‑odd houses away and it just took over. We were hearing people shout, 'Wet your fences, wet your fences'… but there was nothing you could do," Stephens said.

What had started near a park, where overgrown grass and scrubland enabled the fire spread, had quickly travelled through 35 gardens.

"We've lived there for 30 years… and just everything's gone."

In the space of a few hours, the family had lost almost everything they owned.

Among the things destroyed were wedding memorabilia, electronics, clothes and the everyday belongings that had made the house a home.

"It was the kids' childhood home growing up, and everything's gone."

Paul lived there with five other family members, including two children aged seven and nine.

For them, the fire was not simply the loss of a building, but the loss of the place where their family life happened.

When the family returned to see what remained, there was an unexpected small piece of good news - Snowy and Fluffy, the family's two gerbils, had survived.

The pair had been in their enclosure in the downstairs living room as the fire tore through the property.

"The [kids] have one gerbil each, and they survived.

"When we went back the next day, we thought the firemen were bringing out two dead gerbils but they weren't, they were alive."

The family has been staying in temporary Airbnb accommodation while they try to work out what comes next.

Finding somewhere suitable has not been straightforward. Paul has severe neuropathy and needs accommodation that meets his accessibility needs, while also being suitable for a family of six.

"We're being passed from Airbnb to Airbnb at the moment because every house that we go for is not suitable, or for some other reason we can't get it.

"We just need a bit of luck [but we] don't seem to be having any at the moment."

In the meantime, people in the community have stepped in to help.

Clothes have been donated for the family, while the children have received tablets.

"The people in the community… they [have gone] above and beyond. They went and bought them new clothes and tablets and all, because all their computers and stuff and everything was all in there."

Paul and his family are now hoping to find a permanent home to begin rebuilding their life.

articles.title: Bristol airport: Men jailed for 'serious incident' that created 'immense fear'
articles.summary: Police said witnesses believed at the time "this was an active act of terror".
articles.body:
Five men who carried out a serious attack outside Bristol Airport that holidaymakers thought was an "act of terror" have been jailed, police said.

Vladamir Stan, 52, Able Marin, 21, Florin Stan, 28, Constantin Stan, 29, and Emanuel-Ronaldo Dumitru, 27, assaulted two men with bats after crashing into them on 21 February.

The men pleaded guilty to violent disorder at Bristol Crown Court on 28 August and were jailed for a combined 16 years and 10 months.

Det Con Charlotte Couch, from Avon and Somerset Police, said: "We understand the immense fear this incident caused, with witnesses believing at the time this was an active act of terror."

Det Con Ryan Hurt added: "This attack was a serious incident that was targeted and planned, occurring during a Saturday morning at an airport with no thought for anyone else including members of the public."

Police said the 21-year-old victim sustained cuts and bruises to his face and body, and the 37-year-old victim was left with knife wounds.

Bristol Crown Court heard how the five men arrived at the airport at about 08:30 GMT in separate cars and waited for their victims to leave the airport pick-up point.

When the two victims were in their vehicle, the gang targeted the car, colliding with it at a roundabout by the airport entrance on the A38, before getting out of their cars and attacking them using bats.

Det Con Hurt said the defendants and victims are known to each other and added they want to "reassure the public that we do not believe there to be any wider risk".

"The carelessness of those involved has had damaging physical and psychological effects on the victims one of which is still receiving physiotherapy and trying to return to living a normal everyday life," Det Con Hurt added.

Judge Burgess said the attack caused "serious fear and disruption" to other road users and holidaymakers, adding how witnesses thought it was a "terrorist incident" or "car-jacking".

"There was a significant number of resources dispatched to this incident, that responded quickly and efficiently, mitigating further risk and securing the offenders at the earliest opportunity and a number of detectives involved thereafter," Det Con Couch continued.

Vladamir Stan, Marin and Florin Stan also pleaded guilty to possession of an offensive weapon.

Constantin Stan was jailed for four years, having also pleaded guilty to several shoplifting offences.

Vladamir Stan, Florin Stan and Marin were all sentenced to three years and three months in prison. Dumitru was jailed for three years and one month.

articles.title: Donald Trump in Ireland: Huge security operation underway
articles.summary: Gardaí say this is one of the biggest security operations they have ever put in place.
articles.body:
An Garda Síochána (Irish police force) have described preparations for the US president's visit to the Republic of Ireland as "one of the biggest security and policing operations" ever undertaken by them.

The force has declared an extraordinary event and it will see gardaí perform 10,000 12-hour shifts between Friday and Sunday.

US President Donald Trump is expected to touch down on Air Force One at Dublin Airport on Saturday morning for a two-day visit.

There will be disruption and traffic restrictions in Dublin and County Clare.

Gardaí said they have been involved in intense, extensive planning for this policing and security operation over recent weeks.

Two water cannon will be sent from Northern Ireland.

Trump will arrive at Dublin Airport on Saturday 12 September.

He will spend the morning at Phoenix Park, visiting Ireland's President Catherine Connolly at the Áras an Uachtaráin (official residence) and the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House.

Trump is also expected to make a speech at US Ambassador Edward Walsh's Deerfield Residence.

In the afternoon, Trump will be flying into Shannon Airport, County Clare, to attend the Irish Open at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg.

He will leave from the Shannon Airport on Sunday evening.

As a result of the visit, Phoenix Park will be closed to the public until events finish.

That means attractions such as Dublin Zoo and the Magazine Fort will be shut.

Temporary traffic restrictions will be in place on the M50 motorway, with the peak times for these restrictions expected between 08:00-09:00 and 12:00 -13:00 local time, between Junction 3 and 6.

Traffic restrictions are already in place on perimeter roads around Dublin Airport and will remain until Saturday afternoon.

Flight and drone restrictions are also in place around the airport and the Doonbeg golf course.

A temporary maritime exclusion zone and associated outer control area will be in operation in the waters off County Wicklow.

Gardaí have said that normal operations will continue at Dublin Airport and Shannon Airport at all times.

They said members of the public should allow additional time to arrive at the airport due to possible rolling road closures.

At Shannon Airport, there will be additional security checks and passengers should have photo ID and valid flight documentation available for inspection.

Gardaí said access to the areas surrounding Doonbeg village, Trump International Golf Links and Hotel Doonbeg and the wider west Clare areas will be restricted.

Access and traffic along the N67, between Clonadrum Cross (north) and Doonbeg (south) will be restricted from 11 September until the evening of Sunday 13 September.

Protest groups are anticipated at both Shannon Airport and in Doonbeg village.

Only those working at or attending the Irish Open will be allowed to access the Trump International Golf Links and Hotel.

The event can only be accessed via park and ride bus transfers, with no parking or pedestrian access.

There will be airport-style security checks with small bags allowed onsite.

Gardaí said those attending should allow further additional time to arrive and progress through ticket checks and search zones.

articles.title: Alderney Airport to get £24m for runway refurbishment
articles.summary: Further design work is needed following advice and feedback from the States of Alderney.
articles.body:
A major project to rebuild Alderney Airport's ageing runway has been delayed by at least a year, with construction now expected to begin in 2028 rather than 2027.

The delay comes despite politicians approving up to £24m for the scheme in February, when the States of Guernsey had hoped work could start in 2027.

Policy and Resources said further design work was needed after receiving regulatory advice and feedback from the States of Alderney.

The committee said: "Consequently, the design work means that the anticipated milestones set out in the January 2026 policy letter have been revised to reflect this delay, ultimately meaning that construction is now anticipated in 2028, rather than 2027."

The original timetable had envisaged the invitation to tender being issued in March 2026, with the process completed by June.

However, the process has not yet been completed because additional design work is required before construction contracts can be put out to tender, the committee said in a written response to questions from Representative Alexander Snowdon.

Officials said the revised plans would retain the runway's existing width of 18m instead of increasing it to the regulatory standard of 23 metres, a move they said should deliver significant savings. They explained that the approach was being pursued "for the collective financial benefit".

The committee said it was still working towards delivering the project within the current £24m delegated authority, although it warned the budget must also cover costs such as alternative transport and medical evacuation arrangements during construction.

No final completion date has been set. The committee said: "No definitive timeline for the completion of the project can be provided until the contract has been awarded and early contractor engagement has commenced."

Officials said they remained committed to carrying out the work "as soon as is practically possible and at the lowest possible costs, without compromising safety in the meantime".

articles.title: Ryanair boss O'Leary defends 'high-fare rapists' airlines remarks
articles.summary: O'Leary has said airline passengers "can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".
articles.body:
Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists".

Speaking to journalists, O'Leary said some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".

O'Leary doubled-down on his choice of words when asked about them at the time, and later refused to apologise when the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for apology, in a letter seen by the BBC.

Ireland's deputy premier Simon Harris said it was "clearly an inappropriate use of language" and that O'Leary "should have moved to rectify it".

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander told UK radio outlet LBC that victims of rape are "not going to be rushing to book tickets with him, let's be honest".

O'Leary made the comments on Thursday while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders.

Asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate, he said: "Absolutely."

"British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he added.

Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime".

Following O'Leary's comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh wrote to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments.

She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said".

She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise.

"I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote.

In response, O'Leary said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape."

He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training".

It is not the first time O'Leary has offended people while talking about his business .

In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists" in a row over airport charges.

He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories".

In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws.

articles.title: Philippines ferry fire death toll rises to 35 after bodies recovered
articles.summary: Coast Guard says 30 more bodies recovered after five people were initially confirmed dead in Wednesday’s disaster.
articles.body:
Dozens of bodies have been recovered from a ferry that caught fire in the western Palawan province of the Philippines, raising the death toll from the disaster to 35.

According to the Philippine Coast Guard on Friday, 30 bodies were recovered. Earlier, authorities said at least five people had died in the blaze.

On Wednesday, the ferry caught fire on its way from the capital, Manila to Palawan. The vessel had been carrying more than 130 people when it was engulfed in flames.

Fifty-four people are still missing, and there were 43 survivors, authorities said.

Rescuers on Thursday struggled to get inside the vessel because of the heat and smoke, slowing efforts to search for passengers who may have been trapped.

Images provided by the Coast Guard on Friday showed the charred interior of the ship and what appeared to be human remains, ashes and burned metal, including a car.

Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemi Cayabyab said that the burned remains were discovered in the ferry’s economy accommodations. She added that police forensic investigators were examining the remains for recovery and identification.

“We recognise the grief of the families affected by this tragic incident. Rest assured that operations are carried out with utmost respect for the deceased and their bereaved families,” Cayabyab said.

Reporting from Manila on Friday, Al Jazeera’s Jamela Alindogan said a steady number of families are asking about their loved ones and messaging the ferry companies for any information.

“They had better information coming from those who had survived than actually the ferry company,” Alindogan said.

“Much of the information coming from the government and the private sector had been controlled,” she added.

Ferries are frequently used for transport in the Philippine Archipelago. Sea accidents are not uncommon due to storms, badly maintained vessels, overcrowding and spotty enforcement of safety regulations, especially in remote provinces.

“To understand this trip from Manila in the north of the Philippines to the west, it takes over a day. It’s a very long journey, but it is the most affordable mode of transportation for millions of Filipinos,” Alindogan explained, adding that it costs $50 compared with a flight, which would cost $100.

According to the manifest, 134 people were on board, 117 of them passengers and 17 crew. The 53-metre (174-foot) vessel had a capacity to carry 306 passengers and 27 crew. Two passengers listed in the manifest reported to authorities that they failed to board, the Coast Guard said.

It remains unclear what caused the fire, which began as the ferry neared the end of its journey to a popular tourist spot in northern Palawan.

According to a statement from the Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA), citing survivor accounts, two successive explosions were heard inside the ship, triggering the blaze.

articles.title: Houthis claim major advance in Yemen and tighten grip on Red Sea shipping lane
articles.summary: The Iran-backed Houthis are also reported to have seized Perim - a strategic island on the major shipping route.
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthis have claimed a major advance on the western Red Sea coast, consolidating their grip on the key international shipping route.

The Iran-backed group seized Perim Island at the mouth of the waterway in the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a source from Yemen's internationally-recognised government told the BBC.

It comes a day after the Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, according to military sources. A Yemeni military official told the AFP news agency the Houthis now control the entire coastline.

The Houthis earlier said they posed no threat to international shipping but reiterated their threat to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

On Friday, Yemeni pro-government forces withdrew from Perim (also known as Mayyun).

Witnesses and news agencies reported that Houthi forces moved on to the island.

The Houthis later issued a statement, saying that their military operation to expel Saudi-backed forces had been a "success" and that "maritime navigation is safe for all companies except for Saudi vessels".

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Sarea said the "large-scale" military operation was launched on 3 September due to Saudi Arabia's "blatant aggression" against "our dear people".

The statement, however, did not mention Perim Island.

Saudi Arabia has not publicly commented on the latest developments.

Perim Island sits at the narrowest point of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which has become increasingly important following the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz - another crucial waterway - in the conflict between the US and Iran.

Saudi Arabia has been relying on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait for shipping oil to customers in Asia.

The escalation of the conflict between the Houthis, Yemen's government and Saudi Arabia has contributed to a surge in oil prices.

Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-west a week ago.

A Saudi-led coalition has also carried out air strikes on Houthi-controlled areas in western Yemen in support of the pro-government forces, and the Houthis have launched missiles and drones at cities and oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia.

Since fighting escalated, at least 46,000 people have been displaced in Yemen, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

On Friday, the IOM said the number was "alarmingly rising by the hour".

Amy Pope, IOM director general, said: "Families are being forced to flee for the second or third time in this conflict, with almost nothing left."

The Houthis ousted the internationally recognised government in 2015, triggering Saudi military intervention in the civil war. A truce that had largely held for more than four years effectively collapsed in July.

articles.title: Norway's Princess Astrid dies two days after attending brother King Harald's funeral
articles.summary: Princess Astrid "represented the Royal House in a warm and dutiful manner", the new king, Haakon VIII, said in a tribute to his aunt.
articles.body:
Princess Astrid of Norway, the sister of the late King Harald V, has died at the age of 94, two days after attending his funeral, the country's royal palace has announced.

The new king, Haakon VIII, said that "throughout her long life, Princess Astrid represented the Royal House in a warm and dutiful manner".

Harald died last month, aged 89, after more than 35 years as king. His funeral was Astrid's last public engagement.

The princess will be buried at state expense and will be flown at half-mast across Norway, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.

Astrid was the last surviving child of King Olav V, who reigned from 1957 to 1991.

She became Norway's first lady at the age of 22 in 1954, after the death of her mother Crown Princess Märtha. Olav did not remarry and Astrid retained the title until her brother's marriage in 1968.

"In her work, Princess Astrid was always particularly concerned with care and inclusion for the most vulnerable in society," her nephew King Haakon said in his statement.

Her health had deteriorated in recent months and in March she received hospital treatment for pneumonia.

Dozens of European royals and heads of state attended Harald's funeral on Wednesday, including the Prince of Wales and three Nordic kings.

Thousands of people lined the route during a procession from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral on Wednesday afternoon.

The non-royal leaders paying their respects included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier and five foreign prime ministers.

In the final months of Harald's life, Norway's royal family faced personal challenges and scandal.

Earlier this year, documents revealed that his wife, Queen Mette-Marit, had had frequent contact with US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. She later said she wished she had never met the late disgraced financier.

Meanwhile, her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby - who is not a royal but grew up within the family - was given a four-year jail term for two counts of rape in June.

Høiby, who is under house arrest pending appeal, was granted permission to attend the funeral.
